z-m-28-03.title: Number of different arrangements with identical letter cards: compare three solutions
z-m-28-03.topic: Comparing three solutions with identical-looking letter cards mixed in
z-m-28-03.goal: Check if different solutions for arrangements with identical objects are valid, and understand reason for multiplying or dividing steps.
z-m-28-03.material:
There are 6 letter cards. 3 are A, 2 are N, and 1 is B, and cards with the same letter look exactly alike, so they cannot be told apart. Three people solve differently for the number of different letter arrangements (example: BANANA, ABNANA) that can be made by putting the 6 cards in a row.
Seoha: There are 3 kinds of letters, so the way to line up 3 things is 3×2×1=6 ways.
Harin: If we treat all 6 as different, it is 720 ways. Swapping identical letters give the same arrangement, so divide by the 6 orders of the 3 A cards and the 2 orders of the 2 N cards: 720÷12=60 ways.
Junho: There are 20 ways to choose the 3 places out of 6 for A. Among the remaining 3 places, there are 3 ways to choose the 2 places for N. B goes in the remaining place, so 20×3=60 ways.
z-m-28-03.thinking.0: Compare several solutions and judge if dem correct
z-m-28-03.thinking.1: Understand why each multiplication or division happen in solution steps
z-m-28-03.prereq.1: Number of ways to arrange n different things in a row
z-m-28-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all solutions wey correctly find number of different arrangements.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write few arrangements like BANANA and ABNANA, check if Seoha 6 arrangements include all of dem.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.hint.1: Fix B at front, list arrangements of remaining A A A N N directly, then compare with number each solution get.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.r.a: This treat “cards no fit tell apart” as “line up only letter types”. Check by listing if there are 3 A cards and 2 N cards in arrangements.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.r.b: This count as if all 6 different, then divide by repeats from identical ones. E count how many times each object repeat.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.r.c: This decide positions first, then put letters. For identical letter cards, only need choose positions, no need count their order separately.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.explain: Harin divide because 720 arrangements with 6 distinct cards counted each same arrangement 3!×2!=12 times. Junho choose letter positions first, both get 60. Seoha no arrange 6 cards in row, only arrange letter kinds. For example, BANANA and BNAANA look same if only letter-kind order counted.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.prompt: Minjae found, by the same method, the number of different arrangements of 'A 2 cards, B 2 cards, C 1 card' in a row. Which line of the solution is wrong? Line number start from 1.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each line, say if e increase or decrease value from 120.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.hint.1: From line 1, compare if same reason applied to 2 A cards and 2 B cards.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.0: If 5 cards all different, na 5×4×3×2×1=120 arrangements.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.1: Swapping the A cards give the same arrangement, so divide by the 2 orders of the 2 A cards. 120÷2=60 ways.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.2: Swapping the B cards also give the same arrangement, but this time the 2 orders of the 2 B cards are multiplied, giving 60×2=120 ways.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.3: So number of different arrangements na 120.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. Swapping the same B cards also give the same arrangement, so you must divide by 2, exactly as for A. 120÷2÷2=30 ways. When identical cards are mixed in, the number of different arrangements has to be smaller than the 120 ways when all cards are different, and Minjae's result did not get smaller than 120, which also shows something is odd.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.prompt: How many arrangements total for 2 A cards, 2 B cards and 2 C cards in one row?
z-m-28-03.s.s3.hint.0: Say how many times same arrangement repeats for 2 A, 2 B and 2 C cards.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.hint.1: First count how many ways person fit choose positions for the 2 A cards among the 6 positions, then count how many ways person fit choose positions for B among the positions wey remain, and compare dem.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.a: This find result as if all 6 different, then divide by repeats from each card type.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.b: This divided only by the order of the 2 A cards. You need to check whether swapping the identical B and C cards also give the same arrangement.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.c: This value only arrange letter types. It no use fact say each card type get 2.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.d: This divide two times and leave one repeat out. Check if same reason apply to all three types.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.explain: 720÷(2×2×2)=90. Using position method: C(6,2)×C(4,2)×C(2,2)=15×6×1=90 too (meaning multiply ways to choose 2 A positions out of 6, then 2 B positions from remaining 4).

z-m-28-02.title: Two answers come out for 'the number of ways to choose 3 out of 10'
z-m-28-02.topic: Number of cases change based on purpose (whether we distinguish roles)
z-m-28-02.goal: Understand even with same question wording, answer change depending what counts as different case, find what info to check before deciding.
z-m-28-02.material: From 10 students in the broadcasting club, choose 3 to run event. One person no fit take 2 roles. Chaemin talk say '720 ways' and Doha talk say '120 ways,' and both calculate correct. Both answers different because question never tell us something.
z-m-28-02.thinking.1: Stating how we distinguish counted things
z-m-28-02.thinking.2: Seeing how answer change when conditions change
z-m-28-02.prereq.1: Practice deciding the rule to separate 'the same case' from 'a different case' in counting
z-m-28-02.s.s1.prompt: To know which answer correct, wetin we must find first?
z-m-28-02.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate 720÷120, and check if answer equal something countable with 3 people A, B, C.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how many times each answer people would have counted one case in which A, B, and C are chosen.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.a: Whether the 3 chosen people get different roles
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.a: This attitude ask if same three people fit become different case if their roles change. First decide wetin count as same case.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.b: Whether dem choose the 3 people one by one or all together
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.b: This idea treat choosing process as the difference in order. But if same three people chosen, result same even if process differ.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.c: How many of the 10 be third-year students
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.c: Grade mix fit matter if extra conditions dey, but e no explain why current two values differ. First find where two values separate.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.d: Whether same person fit get chosen twice
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.d: Problem already say one person hold only one position. This repeat condition wey dem already give.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.explain: Think of one case in which the three people A, B, and C are chosen. If there are no roles, that is the end of this one case, but if they take different roles, it splits into 6 ways depending on who has which role. 720 is 6 times 120. So 'whether we distinguish roles' is the information that splits the two values.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.prompt: So wetin situation each of 720 and 120 answer? Write one sentence for each situation as real event.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine and write one event where all three people do same work, and one where their work differ.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.hint.1: For each situation, say if choosing A, B and C na same case or different case.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You explain with your own specific words which kind of “distinction” each number count?
z-m-28-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You use same three people A, B, C example to explain how many times one case dey count?
z-m-28-02.s.s2.model.0: Choosing 3 people to do the same work without dividing roles give 120 ways, and deciding different roles such as president, vice president, and secretary give 720 ways. There are 6 ways to divide roles among the same three people, so 720 is 6 times 120.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.model.1: If the 3 people dey one team and we no dey separate who sit for which seat, na 120. If the positions like 1st, 2nd and 3rd place matter, even the same 3 people go count as different cases when the order change, so na 720.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.prompt: This one na new information. Among the 3 people wey dem choose, 1 na the “team leader” and the other 2 na “team members” wey dey do the same work. How many ways person fit choose 1 team leader and 2 team members from 10 people?
z-m-28-02.s.s3.hint.0: Choose three people first, then work out how many ways to pick leader among dem.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare if you get same value when you first choose leader, then choose members from rest.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.a: This count three people without distinguishing dem, even though one na leader. E miss cases where person wey lead change.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.b: This even tells apart the two team members from each other. The team members do the same work, so swapping them give the same case.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.c: This set leader and count only one member. E forget say members suppose be 2.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.d: This judgment count only how many things dem distinguish in a situation where dem distinguish only some things.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.explain: If you choose the three people first, it is 120 ways, and there are 3 ways to choose the team leader among them, so 120×3=360. Counting by deciding the team leader first (10 ways) and then 2 team members out of the remaining 9 (36 ways) also give 10×36=360. Dividing 720 by the order of the two team members (2 ways) give the same value.

z-m-28-12.topic: Make delegation with condition (at least one from each grade): two methods [1]
z-m-28-12.goal: Check count by counting valid arrangements directly and by excluding invalid cases; explain why overlapping count is wrong.
z-m-28-12.material: Debate club has 5 first-years and 4 second-years. Choose 4 with at least one from each grade. Same people count as same delegation; no roles. [1 1 4]
z-m-28-12.thinking.0: Split possible grade makeups without missing cases
z-m-28-12.thinking.1: Check same result by different methods
z-m-28-12.prereq.1: Number ways choose r of n without order
z-m-28-12.s.s1.prompt: Make 3 grade compositions (m first-years,w second-years) satisfying condition. m+w=4; each not exceed grade population.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether m=4 or more, and m=0, satisfy condition.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.ok.c3: Each grade must contribute at least one. [1]
z-m-28-12.s.s1.ok.c4: Neither count can exceed grade population.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.explain: Only compositions (1,3),(2,2),(3,1). Four from one grade fails condition. [1 1 2 2 3 3 3 4 4]
z-m-28-12.s.s2.prompt: For each composition, how many delegations? Add them.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.hint.0: For each, separately choose m of 5 first-years and w of 4 second-years.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.hint.1: Check if delegations from different compositions could be same.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.r.a: Dis count only 2-and-2 composition; other ones missing.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.r.b: Looks like choose one from each grade first, then rest; same delegation counted many times. [1]
z-m-28-12.s.s2.r.c: This chooses any 4 of 9, without excluding single-grade cases.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.r.d: You count each composition separately and add without overlap.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.explain: (1,3): 5×4=20; (2,2):10×6=60; (3,1):10×4=40. Total 120. Different compositions are different delegations. [1 1 2 2 3 3]
z-m-28-12.s.s3.prompt: Check another way: count all, remove cases failing condition. Explain why “choose 1 from each grade, then choose 2 of remaining 7” wrong. [1]
z-m-28-12.s.s3.hint.0: By grade, count delegations containing only that grade.
z-m-28-12.s.s3.hint.1: Count directly how many times delegation first-years A,B and second-years C,D appears in wrong method.
z-m-28-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give example showing how many times one delegation counted?
z-m-28-12.s.s3.model.0: From 126 total groups of 4, subtract 5 all-first-year and 1 all-second-year groups =120. Choosing one from each first makes duplicates, so wrong. [9]
z-m-28-12.s.s3.model.1: Invalid groups are single-grade: 5 ways all first-years, 1 all second-years. 126−6=120. Fixing one of each first counts same delegation repeatedly. [4 4]
z-m-28-12.s.s3.model.2: Subtract C(5,4) and C(4,4) from C(9,4): remove 6, leaving 120. Choosing members sequentially this way duplicates groups.

z-m-28-08.title: Ways to climb stairs: can we trust pattern once noticed?
z-m-28-08.topic: Ways climb 1 or 2 steps (find number pattern and reason)
z-m-28-08.goal: Understand pattern from first few values no fixed, find pattern reason from structure and continue values, and check same value using another method.
z-m-28-08.material: You fit climb 1 or 2 steps each time. For n steps, let a(n) mean number of different ways to climb from bottom to top (read it as 'a of n'). Different step order count as different way. For example, with 3 steps 3 ways dey, 1-1-1, 1-2, and 2-1, so a(3)=3.
z-m-28-08.thinking.0: Guessing pattern from data and knowing its limits
z-m-28-08.thinking.2: Checking same value using other method
z-m-28-08.prereq.1: The rule say different step order be different way, and adding natural numbers
z-m-28-08.s.s1.prompt: Each time new info come, guess value and change guess.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.hint.0: First write how many patterns you fit see from known values.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check if new info reduce estimate to one, or leave several options.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.after: From 3 values 1, 2, 3 alone, both 'it goes up by one each time' (4) and 'the sum of the previous two values' (5) fit happen. For now we no fit choose one.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: I see 1, 2, 3 continuing by going up by one each time.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: I see am as adding the previous two values.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: I see am as multiplying the previous two values. a(3)=3 no fit this rule.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: I think values double every time. This no match 1, 2, 3.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.after: From 1, 2, 3, 5, both 'differences na 1, 1, 2, so next difference na 2' (7) and 'the sum of the previous two values' (8) look natural. Numbers alone still no make am sure.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: I think increase by 1 continue even though the differences 1, 1, 2.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: I think 2 increase come after the differences 1, 1, 2.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: I think add previous 2 values rule continue.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: I think values double every time. This no match 1, 2, 3, 5.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.info: Find the reason. Last step before reach top na 1 or 2 steps. If last step na 1, ways to climb n−1 steps before am na a(n−1), and if e na 2 steps, ways to climb n−2 steps na a(n−2). Both cases no overlap.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: Use this structure, wetin a(5) and a(8) be?
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.after: a(5)=a(4)+a(3)=5+3=8, a(6)=13, a(7)=21, a(8)=34. Now we know reason from structure, number pattern guess don confirm.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: After get 7 from difference rule, I shift number one place wrong and get 21.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: I continue values using case split by final step.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: I use structure up to fifth value, but after that I add 3 each time. 5
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: I think values increase by 5 each time.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.reflect: At first both 4 and 5 (and then 7 and 8) fit happen, but once we know final step be 1 or 2, only one answer remain. Think difference between picking one from number pattern and finding proof reason.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 different ways to climb 8 steps using exactly 5 steps. Each stride na 1 or 2 steps, and different order count as different way. (in order w1, w2, w3, w4, w5)
z-m-28-08.s.s2.hint.0: First find how many of 5 strides must be 2 steps so total 8.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.hint.1: After you choose number of 2-step strides, change only their positions to make new orders.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.explain: For 5 stride total to be 8, exactly 3 strides must be 2 and 2 must be 1. So only positions for both 1-steps change, and 10 ways to choose 2 from 5.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.prompt: How many ways person fit climb 8 steps with exactly 5 strides?
z-m-28-08.s.s3.hint.0: For each way to climb 8 steps with 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 strides, write how many 2-step strides dey inside.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the total wey you get from the number of strides equal the a(8) we calculate before.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.a: This one count only the cases wey the place of the 2-step stride shift by just one.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.b: Na the number of ways to choose where the 1-step strides (or 2-step strides) dey among the 5 strides.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.c: This number separate the order when e dey choose places for the 2-step strides. The same choice of places count many times.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.d: This one na number of ways to choose 2 from 6. Dem mistake the 5 strides for 6.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.explain: If you choose from 5 places where the two 1-step strides go, all the rest go be 2-step strides, so na 10 ways to choose 2 out of 5 places. You fit check am by grouping according to number of strides and add. 4 strides give 1 way, 5 give 10, 6 give 15, 7 give 7, and 8 give 1; altogether na 34 ways, equal to a(8)=34.

z-m-28-06.title: Solution gave 0: which line wrong?
z-m-28-06.topic: Triangles from regular octagon vertices using no octagon side
z-m-28-06.goal: Use small example to show result impossible, find first error line and correct count.
z-m-28-06.material: Regular octagon vertices 1–8 clockwise. Choose 3 for triangle: how many with none of three sides an octagon side (all diagonals)? 8 next to 1; segment between neighbors is side. Doha solution below. [1 2 8 3 8 1]
z-m-28-06.thinking.1: Find wrong line in case-split solution
z-m-28-06.thinking.2: Check by making examples for fixed answer
z-m-28-06.s.s1.prompt: Doha conclusion 0. First error line? Count from 1.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.hint.0: For vertices 1,3,5, count octagon sides used; compare Doha result. [1 3]
z-m-28-06.s.s1.hint.1: For line 3 choose side 1–2; list other 6 vertices and form triangle with each, count sides.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.0: 56 choices of 3 from 8, each triple makes a triangle.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.1: Triangles using 2 octagon sides are 3 consecutive vertices e.g. 1,2,3; 8 cases. [2 1 2 3 8]
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.2: Exactly 1 side: choose side (8 ways), third vertex among 6 non-endpoints: 8×6=48.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.3: Using any side: 8+48=56, so none use no side: 56−56=0.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.explain: Line 3 first error. With side 1–2, other six include 8 next to 1 and 3 next to 2; either makes 2 sides, not “exactly 1.” Only vertices 4,5,6,7 work, so 8×4=32. Zero also suspicious: 1,3,5 makes triangle with no side. [3 1 2 6 1 2 8 1 3 2 2 1 4 4 5 6 7 8 4 32 0 1 3 5]
z-m-28-06.s.s2.prompt: Correct it: make 3 triangles using exactly one side. Used side joins p and p+1 (if p=8, join 8–1); third vertex c.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.hint.0: Vertices next to side p–(p+1) are p−1 and p+2. List vertices left after excluding those and p,p+1.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.hint.1: For chosen c, list all three triangle sides and check if each is octagon side.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.fail.c2: With this c, exactly one side not used? Check if c is endpoint or adjacent to endpoint.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.explain: If choose side 1–2, c must be 4,5,6,7: 4 choices. 8 sides give 32. Three-consecutive-vertex triangles (2 sides) total 8, so triangles using at least one side=40; no-side triangles=56−40=16. [1 2 4 4 5 6 7 8 8 4 32 2 8 32 8 40 56 40 16]
z-m-28-06.s.s3.prompt: With correction, how many triangles total use no side (all diagonals)?
z-m-28-06.s.s3.hint.0: Split 56 into 2-side, exactly-1-side, no-side cases and table them.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.hint.1: Give few examples of triangles whose vertices are not adjacent.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.a: This subtract only triangles using 2 sides. Need subtract exactly-one-side too. [2 1]
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.b: This subtract only exactly-one-side cases. Also subtract 2-side triangles. [1 2]
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.c: You trust first solution. Checking 1,3,5 triangle changes result. [1 3]
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.d: Dis judgment subtract both 2-side and exactly-one-side triangles. [2 1]
z-m-28-06.s.s3.explain: 56−8−32=16. These triples have no adjacent vertices, e.g. 1,3,5. Direct count of 3 from 8 with no adjacent pair also gives 16. [1 3]

z-m-28-04.title: Ways to color map with five regions: estimate change as information come
z-m-28-04.topic: Number of ways to color touching regions different colors (middle region and ring-shaped regions)
z-m-28-04.goal: When neighboring rules appear step by step, update estimated count, divide cases to get exact answer, then apply when number of colors change.
z-m-28-04.material: Imaginary island divide into five regions A, B, C, D, E. A in middle and B, C, D, E around am. B touches C, C touches D, D touches E, and E touches B. B and D no touch; C and E no touch. Touch at one point no count as touching. Touching regions need different colors; no need use all colors.
z-m-28-04.thinking.0: Update estimate when new information come
z-m-28-04.thinking.1: Find overlap between neighboring conditions and split into cases
z-m-28-04.thinking.2: Apply to situation where conditions changed

z-m-28-04.s.s1.prompt: Whenever new information come, estimate number of colorings and update am.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.hint.0: Separate what you know now from what you never check yet.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.hint.1: When coloring one region, count how many touching regions already get color.

z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The 3 colors other than A color
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This use rule say regions touching A must have color different from A.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This limit all four regions to only two colors. Any color different from A color dey allowed.

z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Suppose start coloring from B. I count 3 colors for B, 2 colors for C because e touch B, and 2 for D because e touch C. Now E touch both D and B.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How we fit estimate number of ways to color B, C, D and E?
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.after: 3×2×2×2=24 count case where E only touch D. E touch B too, so real count less than 24. For exact answer, split by whether B and D same color or different.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This value no use any neighboring conditions.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This count as if E only touch one earlier region. E touch two regions.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This estimate account for restriction because E touch two neighbors.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Your estimate too small. You assume each region get almost no colors to choose.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.info:
Split into cases based on whether B and D use same or different colors.
(1) B and D same: C and E no touch each other. Count colors each can use.
(2) B and D different: C must avoid both B and D, and E too. Count colors left for C and E.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: If we include the 4 colours for A, how many ways dey altogether to colour the whole map with 4 colours?
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.after: (1) B has 3 ways, D has 1 way since it has the same color as B, and C and E are each chosen from the 2 colors different from B (and D), so 3×1×2×2=12 ways. (2) B has 3 ways, D has 2 ways different from B, and C and E are each fixed by the 1 remaining color, so 3×2×1×1=6 ways. The ways to color B to E are 18, and multiplying by the 4 colors of A give 72 ways.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You add both cases (12 and 6 ways) to get 18, then multiply by 4 choices for A.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This multiply 4 choices for A by intermediate estimate 24 as e be.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This multiply 4 choices for A by 81, wey no use neighbor conditions.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Dis count only color ways for B–E, no multiply by A 4 colors.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.reflect: First judgment (B–E use only 3 colors) stayed right. Intermediate estimate changed. 24 assumed “only one neighbor”; new info E touch two neighbors made answer smaller. Review whether finding estimate error matter more than calculation.

z-m-28-04.s.s2.model.1: Choose A in 3 ways. If B one of remaining 2, C must be other color, D same as B, E same as C. B choices 2, so 3×2=6. [3 2 3 2 6]

z-m-28-04.s.s2.model.3: A 3 choices × B 2; C,D,E fixed sequentially, total 6.

z-m-28-01.title: The answer wey say 'there na 4000 passwords with 7 inside': wetin look wrong?
z-m-28-01.topic: The mistake in answer counting cases 'with 7 inside' in 4-digit passwords where repetition allowed
z-m-28-01.goal: Use small cases check why choosing one position then filling rest count same password many times, and explain how to get correct count.
z-m-28-01.material: One 4-digit password use digits 0 to 9. Each place fit get digit 0 to 9, same digit fit repeat, and first digit fit be 0 (example: 0707). Below na Seoyun method to solve 'How many passwords get digit 7 at least once?' (This question no relate to real passwords.)
z-m-28-01.thinking.0: Checking line by line wetin each solution line count
z-m-28-01.thinking.1: Testing answer by listing small cases direct
z-m-28-01.thinking.2: Checking whether same thing count multiple times
z-m-28-01.prereq.0: Assume students don learn counting methods (sum rule, product rule, permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.

z-m-28-01.s.s1.hint.0: Follow, with examples, 'which passwords' each line counts. For this method, how many times dem count 0770 wey get 2 sevens?? (7)
z-m-28-01.s.s1.hint.1: When you choose one position in line 2, check wetin happen if 7 show again for the other 3 positions of line 3.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.0: Password get 4 positions, each position fit be 0 to 9, and same digit fit repeat. Total na 10×10×10×10=10000 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.1: To count passwords wey get 7, choose one position for 7. 4 positions dey, so 4 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.2: Put 7 there, and other 3 positions fit get any digit, so 10×10×10=1000 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.3: So number of passwords wey get 7 na 4×1000=4000 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.4: 4000 below total 10000, so answer look reasonable.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 3 together cause problem. If line 2 choose 'one place for the 7' and line 3 allow another 7 for the other 3 positions, then password with 2 or more 7 count once for each position choice. For example, 7777 dem count am 4 times and 0770 is counted 2 times. Line 5 also no be valid reason. A value below total no mean say answer correct.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.prompt: To test solution, I reduce position number and use same method for 2-digit passwords (00 to 99) (2 places for the 7 × 10 ways for the other place). Wetin we learn if we compare this with count from direct listing wey get 7 from 00 to 99?
z-m-28-01.s.s2.hint.0: Among 00 to 99, list separately ones with 7 first and second position. 7
z-m-28-01.s.s2.hint.1: Find passwords wey dey both lists.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.a: Both answers same. If e correct for 2 positions, method trustworthy.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.a: This judgment trust method without listing small case. Only listing and comparing show method mistakes.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.b: Method answer bigger. Number like 77 count twice.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.b: This idea compare table with method count and identify passwords counted twice.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.c: Method answer smaller. Method miss some passwords.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.c: You notice answers different, but no identify missing or double counted. If you compare one by one with direct list, you fit see which one.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.d: Both answers different. But difference go disappear as positions increase.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.d: You no notice as positions increase, passwords with multiple 7s increase, so difference no disappear.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.explain: Direct list for 2 positions give the 10 from 70 to 79 and the 10 of 07, 17, ..., 97, but 77 dey in both, so total 19. Method answer na 2×10=20, so 77 count twice, once because 'first place is 7' and once because 'second place is 7.' For 4 positions more passwords get 2 or more 7s, so difference bigger.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.prompt: Write one correct method to find number of 4-digit passwords containing a 7 at least once, and calculate answer. Also explain in one sentence how Seoyun method count password like 7777 many times.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.hint.0: Count how many times passwords with multiple 7s, like 7777 or 0770, get counted in Seoyun's method.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.hint.1: First count passwords with no 7, and think how e connect to question.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You check whether your answer match direct list for small case like 2 positions?
z-m-28-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You explain “counted plenty times” with one exact password like 7777?
z-m-28-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You choose either splitting by number of 7s or counting no-7 case, and calculate fully?
z-m-28-01.s.s3.model.0: 7777 count once for each of 4 position choices, so it dem count am 4 times. Remove 9×9×9×9=6561 no-7 cases from total 10000 ways give 3439 ways. 7
z-m-28-01.s.s3.model.1: After choosing position, if another 7 go in other positions, same password count again. So divide cases by 7-count and add. Add 4×729 for one 7, 6×81 for two, 4×9 for three, and 1 for four give 3439 ways.

z-m-28-05.title: Test claim “with 10 points, always 120 triangles”
z-m-28-05.topic: Triangles from 10 plane points when some collinear
z-m-28-05.goal: Find condition for claim, arrange points violating it and count triangles; explain count change.
z-m-28-05.material: 10 plane points; triangle from 3 vertices only if not collinear. Same vertices same triangle. Jihu says “10 points always make 120 triangles.” Consider arrangement where k≥3 points lie on one line, and no other three collinear. [10 10 120 10 3]
z-m-28-05.thinking.0: Find condition for claim to hold
z-m-28-05.thinking.2: Explain how result changes with variable
z-m-28-05.s.s1.prompt: How should we judge Jihu claim?
z-m-28-05.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine 4 points collinear and other 6 off line; find which triples among those 4 make triangle.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write condition needed for number of 3-point choices to equal triangle count. []
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.a: You assume choosing 3 always makes triangle. Check that. []
z-m-28-05.s.s1.o.b: Depending on positions, more than 120 because one point used in multiple triangles.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.b: You mistake repeated point participation for extra count. Triangle determined by one triple; choices are upper bound.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.o.c: Could be fewer than 120: collinear triples no triangle.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.c: You find condition: some triples do not form triangles.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.o.d: Cannot tell without picture of positions.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.d: Even without picture, set positions in words and test.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.explain: Choices C(10,3)=120, but collinear triples no triangle. If no 3 collinear, 120; if some collinear, fewer. Need condition no three collinear. [10 3 120 3 10 120 120]
z-m-28-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose k collinear among 10, find triangle count t, give 3 different k examples (3–10).
z-m-28-05.s.s2.hint.0: For k=3, first count how many triangles that collinear triple cannot make.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.hint.1: For k=4,5 list triples among line points and count. [4 5]
z-m-28-05.s.s2.fail.c2: t wrong. Check how you count triples from k line points.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.ok.c3: Less than 120, so counterexample to Jihu.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.explain: k=3 gives119, k=4 116, k=5 110, k=6 100. Collinear triples count k(k−1)(k−2)/6 and do not form triangle, subtract from 120. Counting by 0,1,2 line-points gives same; k=4:20+60+36=116. [3 119 4 116 5 110 6 100 1 2 6 120 0 1 2 4 20 60 36 116]
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.prompt: As k grow, how t change? Brief reason.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare k,t in your two examples.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: How many extra non-triangle triples appear when k increases by 1?
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you state direction and give numerical example?
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain collinear triples no triangle?
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.model.0: As k grow, t decrease. More choices of 3 among collinear points fail, so more subtracted from 120. []
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.model.1: It decreases: 119 at k=3, 116 at 4, 110 at 5. Collinear points cannot make triangle, and such triples increase with k.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.model.2: As k increase, t decrease; any 3 points on one line cannot form triangle. []

z-m-28-09.title: We don find solutions wey get x<y<z; if we remove that order condition, how many solutions go dey?
z-m-28-09.topic: Three different natural numbers wey total 12: one condition fix their order, the other one no fix am.
z-m-28-09.goal: Find all the solutions wey meet the condition in an organized way, and explain how fixing or removing the order condition affect the number of solutions.
z-m-28-09.material: Different natural numbers x, y, z satisfy x<y<z and x+y+z=12. Natural numbers na 1, 2, 3, ... For example, (1, 2, 9) satisfy the condition.
z-m-28-09.thinking.0: Build the different solutions wey satisfy the conditions.
z-m-28-09.thinking.1: Choose a method wey go find all of dem without missing any.

z-m-28-09.s.s1.prompt: Make 5 different (x, y, z) triples wey satisfy the condition.

z-m-28-09.s.s2.prompt: Wetin be the best way to check say you find all of dem without missing any?

z-m-28-09.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether any solution dey when x=4, then decide where to stop.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.a: Set x to 1, 2, 3, ... one by one, then check pairs wey satisfy y<z.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.a: You use the idea say if you fix one variable each time and check the others, you fit know how far you don go.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.b: Count only the values of x, assuming say when x don fixed, y and z get only one choice.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.b: Even when x na just 1, y and z fit get plenty pairs. You assume say dem get only one.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.c: For every solution wey you find, also add the ones wey swap x, y and z as new solutions, then count dem.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.c: The condition x<y<z don already fix the order. The swapped ones break the condition, so dem no be solutions.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.d: Start by setting z as the biggest value, 12, then check while you reduce x and y.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.d: If z na 12, then x+y=0, so no natural-number solution dey. You no check the possible range when you start from the biggest number.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.explain: If x=1, y+z=11 and 4 pairs satisfy y<z; if x=2, y+z=10 and 2 pairs get y≥3; if x=3, y+z=9 and 1 pair get y≥4; if x=4 or more, no solution dey. Altogether na 7.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.prompt: Now remove the condition x<y<z, and na enough that x, y, z are different natural numbers with x+y+z=12 ((9, 1, 2) is also a solution). How many solutions are there in all? Write the value and the reason.

z-m-28-09.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether solutions wey swap the numbers differ from one another, and whether dem overlap with solutions from other groups.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You explain how many different orders one group of 3 different numbers fit get?
z-m-28-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You explain why you multiply all 7 groups by the same number (each group get the same 6 orders)?
z-m-28-09.s.s3.model.0: Each of the 7 solutions with x<y<z get 6 different orders to arrange the 3 numbers, and because the numbers differ, every arrangement na a different solution. So 7×6=42.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.model.1: You fit arrange one group of 3 numbers like {1, 2, 9} into (x, y, z) in 3×2×1=6 ways; so for all 7 groups, na 42 ways.

z-m-28-10.title: CBEAD na number 58 or 59?
z-m-28-10.topic: Find the position of a word when words dey arranged in dictionary order (alphabetical order).
z-m-28-10.goal: Check the relationship between 'the number of words before it' and 'which position na' with a small case, judge which of the two people's calculations is valid, and apply it to the reverse problem (finding the word from the number).
z-m-28-10.material:
Using each of the five letters A, B, C, D, and E exactly once to make 5-letter words and listing them all in dictionary order (alphabetical order) gives 120 words. The first word is ABCDE, the second is ABCED, and the last is EDCBA. Jiwon and Taemin found which position the word 'CBEAD' is.
Jiwon: Count 24 words starting with A, 24 words starting with B, 6 words starting with C whose second letter is A, 2 words starting with CBA, and 2 words starting with CBD. 24+24+6+2+2=58, so na the 58th.
Taemin: After counting the same words as Jiwon, he says na the 59th.
z-m-28-10.thinking.0: Find the difference between two calculations and judge the result.
z-m-28-10.thinking.1: Test your judgment with a small example.
z-m-28-10.thinking.2: Use the same pattern for a problem wey reverse the direction.
z-m-28-10.prereq.1: The number of ways to arrange n different things in a row (n!).
z-m-28-10.s.s1.prompt: Which person get the correct value: 58 or 59?
z-m-28-10.s.s1.hint.0: Group the words wey come before CBEAD according to their first letter, in order, and write how many dey for each group.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.hint.1: Explain in one sentence wetin 58 dey count.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.a: Jiwon dey correct. The number wey count the words before CBEAD na the position itself.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.a: This treats 'how many are before it' and 'which position na' as the same. You did not check the relationship between the two with a small case.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.b: Both of dem dey wrong. All 24 words wey start with C must come before am.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.b: You miss say na only the words starting with C wey come before CBEAD dem dey count.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.c: We no fit know. We no go settle am until we list all 120 words.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.c: If you count by splitting into groups, you fit settle am without listing everything. You no use the method wey judge without listing.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.d: Taemin is right. There are 58 words before it, so na the next one, the 59th.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.d: You judge am based on how the number before am relate to its position.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.explain: The words before CBEAD are 24 starting with A, 24 starting with B, 6 starting with CA, 2 starting with CBA, and 2 starting with CBD, 58 in all. CBEAD comes first of the two words starting with CBE (CBEAD, CBEDA), so na the next one, the 59th. Jiwon's 58 is the number of words before CBEAD.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.prompt: Check with small example. List in alphabetical order 6 words using letters A, B, C once, and find CAB position. Write connection between position and number of words before CAB, and and say whose method correct.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare words before CAB with CAB position, and compare them.

z-m-28-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You connect this to CBEAD case and decide which person correct?
z-m-28-10.s.s2.model.0: Order na ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA, so CAB na 5th. 4 words before CAB dey, so position na number before plus 1. So if there are 58 before CBEAD, na the 59th, so Taemin correct.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.model.1: Listing 6 words, CAB is the fifth. 4 words dey before am, so 'which position' counts up to the word itself and is 5. Jiwon use count before word as position.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.model.2: CAB is fifth and there are 4 before it. Position na one more than words before, so CBEAD, 58 words later, is 59th, so Taemin correct.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.prompt: When 120 5-letter words list alphabetically, wetin be 100th word?

z-m-28-13.s.s2.selfAssess.3: Did you explain notation friend may not know?
z-m-28-13.s.s2.model.0: Fix A. If chosen, choose 2 of other 9 =C(9,2); if not, choose 3 of 9 =C(9,3). Both cannot happen simultaneously, so disjoint, and every group is one case. Add counts to get C(10,3).
z-m-28-13.s.s2.model.1: Split teams of 3 from 10 into those containing A and not containing A. With A choose 2 from remaining 9; without choose 3. No team can both contain and not contain A, and all teams fit one group. [3 3 9]
z-m-28-13.s.s2.model.2: If chosen, choose 2 of other 9=C(9,2); if not, choose 3=C(9,3). No team overlap; together all teams. [9]
z-m-28-13.s.s3.prompt: Apply same method to C(12,5). What equal? [12 5]
z-m-28-13.s.s3.hint.0: For 5 of 12, state choose-from and choose-how-many in A-in and A-out cases.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.hint.1: Compare option number pairs with two cases above.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.r.a: You transfer rule: A in => 4 of 11; A out => 5 of 11.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.r.b: If A chosen, choose 4 from 11, but you reused 4 for A not chosen. There choose 5 from 11.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.r.c: You multiply cases instead of adding. They are mutually exclusive alternatives.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.r.d: You use same choose-count in both cases. If A included, one fewer slot remains.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.explain: A chosen: C(11,4); not chosen: C(11,5). Disjoint and complete, add: 330+462=792=C(12,5). [11 11 4 5]

z-m-28-11.title: Testing claim 'there are only 3 tie cases'
z-m-28-11.topic: Rock-paper-scissors played by 3 people together: counting result groups
z-m-28-11.goal: Test claim with counterexample, and split all cases into separate result groups and count to make sure total match.
z-m-28-11.material: 3 people A, B, C each show scissors, rock, or paper together. Scissors beats paper, rock beats scissors, and paper beats rock. Write choices in order (A, B, C) to separate cases (example: (scissors, scissors, paper) and (scissors, paper, scissors) different cases). Results split into 3 types. If one person choice beat both other choices, na 'one wins'; if 2 people with same choice beat the remaining person, na 'two win'; otherwise na a 'tie.' Eunwoo said, 'Total 27 dey, and tie only happen when all 3 show same thing, so there be 3.'
z-m-28-11.thinking.1: Making cases that meet condition yourself
z-m-28-11.thinking.2: Splitting all cases into groups and checking total
z-m-28-11.prereq.1: Counting cases: separating by ordered pairs
z-m-28-11.s.s1.prompt: How you go judge Eunwoo statement?
z-m-28-11.s.s1.hint.0: When each person choose different one from scissors, rock, paper, write who beat who.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.hint.1: Find cases among 'the three are not all the same' where nobody win.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.a: E correct. If three players show different things, surely somebody win.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.a: You only notice “different” and no check who wins against who. Write directly who beats who when all three show different signs.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.b: E wrong. Case where all three differ also fit be tie.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.b: You think how all-different case has nobody beating both others, and make counterexample.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.c: E correct. Three people have 3×3×3 possible signs, so ties at most 3.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.c: You set unsupported upper limit between all cases and tie cases.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.d: E wrong. Remaining 24 cases besides all-same are ties.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.d: You see counterexample but no check other cases can still have winner.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.explain: If all show different, like (scissors,rock,paper), scissors beat paper but lose to rock, so nobody beat both others: tie. Such case count as tie, so Eunwoo wrong.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 cases where matching pair beat third (“two win”), like rock beat scissors. Code scissors=1, rock=2, paper=3.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.hint.0: Two winners show same thing. Choose their sign first, then third shows sign it loses to.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.hint.1: Scissors beat paper, rock beat scissors, paper beat rock. Check how relation appear with 1,2,3. [1 2]
z-m-28-11.s.s2.ok.c2: Exactly two people show same thing.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.fail.c2: Exactly two people must show same thing.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.ok.c3: The matching pair beat the remaining person.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.fail.c3: The matching pair no beat the third. Check scissors>paper, rock>scissors, paper>rock.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.explain: Matching pair can choose 3 signs; third sign then fixed. Any of A,B,C can lose (3 choices), so 3×3=9.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.prompt: Split 27 cases into tie, one winner, two winners and count: wetin you get?
z-m-28-11.s.s3.hint.0: For one-winner cases, choose winner and their sign, then see remaining signs fixed.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.hint.1: Check if three group totals add to 27, with no overlap or missing cases.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.a: Keeps first tie count 3 and splits remaining cases in half.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.b: This tie count miss all-same cases.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.c: You count ties (3 all-same + 6 all-different), then two winner groups separately.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.d: Ties correct but one winner group wrong; totals merely made to match.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.explain: Ties: 3 all-same plus 3×2×1=6 all-different, total 9. One winner: choose winner (3) and their sign (3), total 9. Two winners also 3×3=9. Total 27. [3 3 9 9 9]

z-m-28-07.prereq.0: Assume students don learn counting methods (sum rule, product rule, permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-07.title: Interpret record that applicants 22+25=47
z-m-28-07.topic: Interpret apparently contradictory activity applicant sum and total people
z-m-28-07.goal: Explain sum applicants can exceed people total, make possible distributions, judge extra info fixing number.
z-m-28-07.material: 40 club students asked sign up activities. 22 apply swimming, 25 hiking; one student can apply both. Teacher records “swimming or hiking applicants 22+25=47.”
z-m-28-07.s.s1.prompt: Looking at 47 and 40 together, best interpretation?
z-m-28-07.s.s1.hint.0: How many times student applying to both counted in 22+25?
z-m-28-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write what 40 students count and what 47 applications count.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.o.a: Data wrong: 47 applicants impossible with 40 students. [40 47]
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.a: You miss one student can apply both.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.b: You read excess as non-applicants; larger sum may come from double-counting.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.o.c: Some applied both, so 47 counts applications, not students.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.c: You consider double-count possibility and combine data with condition.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.o.d: Maybe student total no be 40. 22+25=47, so 47 students. [40 22 25 47]
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.d: You change given 40 to preserve conclusion; but 40 fixed.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.explain: If student applies both, counted twice in sum. Sum above total not strange; 47 counts applications, not people. [22 25 47]
z-m-28-07.s.s2.prompt: Assume all data true; each of 40 either swimming only, hiking only, both, neither. Make 3 possible (b,n): b both, n neither.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.hint.0: Split into four groups and express counts using b,n.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.hint.1: If b of 22 swimming applicants apply both, how many swimming-only?
z-m-28-07.s.s2.ok.c2: Both applicants at most 22 swimming applicants.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Both count cannot exceed 22 swimming applicants.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.ok.c3: At least-one applicants plus neither sum to 40.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Those two counts no total 40. Express at-least-one using b.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.explain: b,n satisfy n=b−7 and 7≤b≤22. (7,0): everyone applies, overlap 7. (22,15): all swimmers also hikers, 15 apply neither. Data no fix unique pair. [7 7 22 7 0 7 22 15 22 15]
z-m-28-07.s.s3.prompt: Teacher wants number of students applying swimming or hiking. Which single info below would fix count if only that is known?
z-m-28-07.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, see which of four group counts become fixed.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.hint.1: Test whether b can be found from each single value.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.a: You remember 22 swimming total minus swimming-only gives overlap.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.b: Grade counts no tell activity overlap.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.c: You recall total 40 minus neither immediately gives number applying.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.o.d: Number whose first application was swimming
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.e: You recall knowing overlap lets subtract it from total 47. []
z-m-28-07.s.s3.explain: If s swimming-only, overlap=22−s and union=25+s. If n neither, union=40−n. If b both, union=47−b. Grade distribution or application order no fix overlap.
